extracted.intended_audience: readers and commenters of Retraction Watch; people who want to report suspected research misconduct or alert RW to retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Site-specific FAQ and comments policy describing what kinds of comments and tips Retraction Watch will accept, how they moderate, and how to report suspected misconduct or retractions to them or to journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ad hominem attacks or personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: We will not tolerate ad hominem attacks, personal attacks, and similar material in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site editors state that such attacks 'destroy the discourse' and are removed/unapproved; commenters should avoid personal attacks and rewrite comments to remove them if necessary. Repeated or severe violations may lead to unapproval and contact from editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unfounded allegations, unverified facts, or speculation (no mind‑reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: We will not tolerate unfounded allegations and unverified facts — a category that includes speculation, whether about what might have happened, or about the mindset of the people involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If verifying your comment requires mind‑reading or knowing the motivations of people involved, it is unlikely to be approved. Provide verifiable facts and avoid conjecture about intent or motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: No approval of comments containing violating material (no partial approval / no editorial fixes)
rubrics_metrics.description: We will not edit comments, and will not approve any that contain material that violates this policy, even if it is a small part of a larger comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the editors have sometimes had to edit or unapprove comments in the past, the stated policy is not to edit comments to remove violating parts and then approve — commenters should submit compliant versions. If a submitted comment includes disallowed material it will not be approved; users should rewrite and resubmit.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to ask why a comment was not approved
rubrics_metrics.description: Users may contact Retraction Watch to ask why a given comment was not approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the email addresses provided in the About pages and include a working email address; the editors may respond, time permitting. Avoid posting meta-comments on the site asking why another comment was not approved — they may respond to those too if the requester used a working email address.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to submit tips about possible retractions/misconduct to Retraction Watch
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving a comment pointing out a retraction or emailing the editorial addresses are acceptable ways to tip Retraction Watch about potential retractions or misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAQ notes that leaving a comment works and emailing (addresses on the About pages or [email protected] as cited) also works; editors may ask for documents and other material to investigate and cover a story. Provide links to notices or relevant documents to make it easier for the team to follow up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction Watch will not give case‑specific advice or advocate for/against retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: As a journalism organization, Retraction Watch cannot offer advice in specific cases, and cannot advocate for or against a retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They compare giving case‑specific advice to a business reporter recommending stocks; they will suggest other resources when feasible but must preserve editorial independence. Do not expect procedural/legal guidance or representation from the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations about coverage and resource limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage choices are shaped by resources and expertise: the site focuses on current retractions and has deeper coverage in the life sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAQ explains they launched in 2010 and try to keep up with retractions as they happen rather than comprehensively covering historical retractions. They welcome tips for undercovered areas (e.g., physical sciences) but cannot promise coverage for every tip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking/citation practice when reporting retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction Watch typically links to the retraction notice or relevant source; including full citations is helpful but not always provided due to resource constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors say they 'do always link to the notice' and that including DOIs/PMIDs/links helps. Full bibliographic citation may not always be added because it takes extra steps, so tipsters should include clear links or identifiers to make detection easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended method for reporting concerns to journals (COPE‑aligned advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: When notifying journals about potential problems, best practices include contacting authors and editors and following COPE guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approaches from commenters (endorsed in the thread) include: write the authors and request an explanation while cc'ing the editor; or write the editor and cc the authors requesting investigation/correction/retraction. Consider whether to submit a signed letter for publication or an anonymous one clearly marked NOT for publication. Per COPE, journals that publish corrections or retractions are supposed to acknowledge by name whoever brought the issues to their attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of external tools and databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside resources and indexes (e.g., PubPeer, Crossref, PubMed tags, Turnitin reports, compare‑trials.org) can help detect and document problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAQ and comment thread point readers to existing resources (Retraction Watch Database, PubPeer, PubMed retraction tagging, trial‑comparison projects) and note that tipsters can use these tools to assemble evidence to make reports easier to follow up on.
